Low-Rank Masking for Single-Server Matrix Multiplication

Alejandro Cohen    Rafael G. L. D’Oliveira    Alex Sprintson
Abstract

We study the statistical privacy of outsourcing matrix multiplication over a finite field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} to a single server using additive masks of rank at most rr. For independent uniform n×nn\times n inputs, we show that uniform rank-ball masks and products of independent uniform factors give maximal-correlation secrecy of at most q−rq^{-r} against the complete server view, with O⁡(n2​r)O(n^{2}r) field operations for encoding and decoding. This secrecy captures how effectively the server is prevented from estimating functions of the inputs. We prove an asymptotically matching lower bound of this secrecy measure for r=o⁡(n)r=o(n), showing that both sampling methods are asymptotically optimal among input-independent additive masks of rank at most rr, even when secret invertible transformations are allowed. We also characterize the posterior distribution for uniform rank-ball masks under arbitrary joint input distributions and prove approximate individual security for rows and columns under independent uniform inputs. Finally, we show that every input-independent additive mask of rank at most r=o⁡(n)r=o(n) requires δ→1\delta\to 1 in entry-level (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-differential privacy for fixed field size qq and bounded ε\varepsilon.

Index Terms: 
Matrix multiplication, secure outsourcing, distributed computing, individual security.

1 Introduction

We consider a user who has two matrices A∈𝔽qm×nA\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{m\times n} and B∈𝔽qn×pB\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n\times p} and wishes to compute A⋅BA\cdot B with the assistance of a single server. The challenge is to limit what the server learns about AA and BB while keeping the user’s encoding and recovery costs substantially below the cost of computing A​BAB locally.

Homomorphic encryption and specialized cryptographic protocols can protect inputs when outsourcing to a single server, but their privacy guarantees rely on computational hardness assumptions [4, 6]. Secure distributed matrix multiplication (SDMM) achieves perfect information-theoretic privacy against computationally unbounded servers, but requires multiple servers and a bound on how many may collude [12]. The privacy guarantees of these SDMM schemes do not hold when a single server receives all the encoded inputs.

This motivates the transformation-based outsourcing approach [3, 2, 1], in which the user masks the inputs before sending them to the server and recovers the desired product from the returned result. For example, the user can upload P1​A​P2−1P_{1}AP_{2}^{-1} and P2​B​P3−1P_{2}BP_{3}^{-1}, where P1,P2,P3P_{1},P_{2},P_{3} are secret invertible matrices. The server then returns P1​A​B​P3−1P_{1}ABP_{3}^{-1}. Using permutations and scalings makes encoding and recovery inexpensive. This line of work includes sparse-matrix protocols [15], invertible transformations [17, 26, 19, 20], and additive masks [3, 13, 16].

We focus on low-rank additive masking, which has been used for linear systems [22], matrix multiplication [13, 24], and secure inference [25]. Blockwise variants use outer-product masks [16]. For n×nn\times n inputs, each mask of rank at most rr can be written as the product of an n×rn\times r matrix and an r×nr\times n matrix. Using these factors, the user can encode the inputs and recover their product with O⁡(n2​r)O(n^{2}r) field operations, while the server performs one matrix multiplication.

We then ask what statistical privacy these masks can provide. We first consider differential privacy (DP) [11], which limits how much the distribution of the server’s observation can change when one input entry changes. However, Proposition 1 shows that every input-independent mask of rank at most r=o⁡(n)r=o(n) requires δ→1\delta\to 1 in entry-level (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-differential privacy when qq is fixed and ε\varepsilon is bounded.

Thus, we study partial privacy guarantees. We consider two sampling methods: multiplying independent uniform factors and choosing a mask uniformly from all matrices of rank at most rr. For each, we describe which inputs remain possible after the server sees the uploads and how likely they are.

Each input must lie within rank distance rr of its upload (Definition 1). For uniform rank-ball masks, the uploads rule out incompatible input pairs while preserving the relative probabilities of those that remain. Theorem 2 establishes this for arbitrary joint input distributions. For independent uniform matrices, Theorem 3 gives an approximate form of individual security [9] for rows and columns.

Our main result concerns maximal-correlation secrecy [18], which quantifies how well the server can estimate functions of the inputs. For independent uniform square inputs, Theorem 4 gives maximal correlation at most q−rq^{-r} against the complete server view for both sampling methods, with equality for independent uniform factors. Theorem 5 gives an asymptotically matching lower bound for every input-independent additive mask of rank at most rr, even when combined with secret invertible transformations. Thus, for fixed qq and r=o⁡(n)r=o(n), both sampling methods achieve asymptotically optimal maximal-correlation secrecy within this class.

To our knowledge, this is the first work to establish asymptotically matching achievability and converse bounds for maximal-correlation secrecy of input-independent additive matrix masks under a rank constraint with uniform inputs.

1.1 Related Work

Other single-server work considers adjustable security and efficiency [27]. The scheme in [8] combines low-rank factors with additional noise to obtain computational security and allows approximate recovery. The additional noise means that the complete masks need not satisfy the rank constraint studied here. Over the real and complex numbers, analog SDMM studies numerical stability and mutual-information leakage [21], while differentially private distributed multiplication studies privacy–accuracy tradeoffs [10, 7]. In our setting, the user recovers the finite-field product exactly, and we study the uncertainty that remains about the inputs. Individual secrecy protects each message separately while allowing information about relationships between messages. This notion has been studied in secure network coding [9], distributed storage [14], and multi-secret sharing [5].

2 Main Results

We study privacy against a computationally unbounded honest-but-curious (semi-honest [26]) server. Correctness assumes that the server follows the prescribed computation; verifiability against malicious computation is outside the scope of this work. Proofs appear in Section 3.

2.1 Low-Rank Masking

We consider a user who wishes to multiply A∈𝔽qm×nA\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{m\times n} and B∈𝔽qn×pB\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n\times p} with the help of a single server. The user adds a low-rank mask to each matrix before sending it to the server. Let 1≤r≤min⁡{m,n,p}1\leq r\leq\min\{m,n,p\} and R=U​VR=UV and S=Q​WS=QW, where U∈𝔽qm×rU\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{m\times r}, V∈𝔽qr×nV\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{r\times n}, Q∈𝔽qn×rQ\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n\times r}, and W∈𝔽qr×pW\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{r\times p}. The masks are kept secret and sampled independently of the inputs and of each other, with fresh masks for each multiplication. Algorithm 1 describes the protocol.

Theorem 1.

Given the mask factors, Algorithm 1 computes A​BAB using O⁡(m​n​r+n​p​r+m​p​r)O(mnr+npr+mpr) field operations at the user in the worst case and one matrix multiplication at the server.

Example 1.

For n×nn\times n inputs, decoding computes A​QAQ, (A​Q)​W(AQ)W, V​BVB, and U⁡(V​B)U(VB), each using n2​rn^{2}r field multiplications. Decoding therefore requires 4​n2​r4n^{2}r multiplications, while encoding requires O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) additions. Precomputing RR and SS uses 2​n2​r2n^{2}r multiplications, and computing R​SRS as U⁡((V​Q)​W)U((VQ)W) uses another n2​r+2​n​r2n^{2}r+2nr^{2}. Thus, the user’s computation is quadratic in nn for constant rr and o⁡(n3)o(n^{3}) when r=o⁡(n)r=o(n).

2.2 Privacy within Rank Balls

We now ask which inputs remain possible after the server sees an upload and how likely they are. Since X=A+RX=A+R and rank⁡(R)≤r\operatorname{rank}(R)\leq r, observing X=xX=x tells the server that rank⁡(x−A)≤r\operatorname{rank}(x-A)\leq r. We use the rank distance.

Definition 1.

The rank distance between a,x∈𝔽qd×ea,x\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{d\times e} is rank⁡(x−a)\operatorname{rank}(x-a). The rank ball of radius rr centered at xx is Ballr⁡(x)={a∈𝔽qd×e:rank⁡(x−a)≤r}\operatorname{Ball}_{r}(x)=\{a\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{d\times e}:\operatorname{rank}(x-a)\leq r\}.

We consider two ways to sample the masks. Low-Rank Ball samples RR uniformly from Ballr⁡(0)\operatorname{Ball}_{r}(0) and keeps a factorization R=U​VR=UV for decoding. Low-Rank Factors samples all entries of U,VU,V independently and uniformly and sets R=U​VR=UV. Both methods can produce every mask of rank at most rr, but assign different probabilities to them.

After observing X=xX=x, the conditional probability of each input aa is proportional to Pr[A=a]Pr[R=x−a]\Pr[A=a]\Pr[R=x-a]. For uniform rank-ball masks, the second factor is the same for every a∈Ballr⁡(x)a\in\operatorname{Ball}_{r}(x), giving the following result.

Theorem 2.

Let AA have any distribution and let RR be a Low-Rank Ball mask independent of AA. For every upload xx with positive probability,

Pr⁡[A=a∣X=x]=Pr[A=a] 1{a∈Ballr(x)}Pr[A∈Ballr(x)].\Pr[A=a\mid X=x]=\frac{\Pr[A=a]\,\mathbf{1}\{a\in\operatorname{Ball}_{r}(x)\}}{\Pr[A\in\operatorname{Ball}_{r}(x)]}. (1)

For A,BA,B with any joint distribution and Low-Rank Ball masks sampled independently of each other and of (A,B)(A,B), the posterior after uploads x,yx,y of positive joint probability is the joint prior restricted to Ballr⁡(x)×Ballr⁡(y)\operatorname{Ball}_{r}(x)\times\operatorname{Ball}_{r}(y) and normalized.

For uniform rank-ball masks, an upload xx rules out inputs at rank distance greater than rr from xx and preserves the relative probabilities of those that remain. If only one of these inputs has positive prior probability, the server can identify it. Two inputs within rank distance rr of the same upload can still have different upload distributions, since each produces uploads in a rank ball centered at itself.

2.3 Limits on Differential Privacy

We now show that low-rank masking cannot provide useful differential privacy when r=o⁡(n)r=o(n). This limitation comes from the rank bound and holds for every input-independent mask distribution.

Definition 2 ([11] ).

Two inputs are neighbors if they differ in exactly one entry. For ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 and δ∈[0,1]\delta\in[0,1], the upload XX satisfies entry-level (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-differential privacy if

Pr⁡[X∈ℰ∣A=a]≤eε​Pr⁡[X∈ℰ∣A=a′]+δ\Pr[X\in\mathcal{E}\mid A=a]\leq e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[X\in\mathcal{E}\mid A=a^{\prime}]+\delta

for every set of uploads ℰ\mathcal{E} and every pair of neighboring inputs a,a′a,a^{\prime}. The case δ=0\delta=0 is called pure differential privacy.

The following bound holds for every input-independent mask distribution with rank at most rr.

Proposition 1.

Let K∈𝔽qn×nK\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n\times n} be independent of the input, with rank⁡(K)≤r<n\operatorname{rank}(K)\leq r<n almost surely. If A+KA+K satisfies entry-level (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-differential privacy, then

δ≥1−(eε+q−1)​log2​qq−1​rn.\delta\geq 1-\frac{(e^{\varepsilon}+q-1)\log_{2}q}{q-1}\frac{r}{n}. (2)

No such mask gives pure differential privacy for any finite ε\varepsilon.

For fixed qq and bounded ε\varepsilon, the bound forces δ→1\delta\to 1 when r=o⁡(n)r=o(n). At δ=1\delta=1, the privacy condition places no restriction on the upload distribution. Thus, no choice of input-independent mask distribution can give useful differential privacy in this regime.

2.4 Approximate Individual Security

We next ask how much the upload reveals about each row or column separately. We take AA to be uniform over 𝔽qn×n\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n\times n}, let 1≤r<n1\leq r<n, and write X=A+RX=A+R, where RR is independent of AA. We regard the rows Mi=Ai,:∈𝔽qnM_{i}=A_{i,:}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} as independent uniform messages.

Definition 3 ([9]).

For T⊆[n]T\subseteq[n], let MT=(Mi)i∈TM_{T}=(M_{i})_{i\in T}. The messages M1,…,MnM_{1},\ldots,M_{n} satisfy TT-individual security with respect to XX if MTM_{T} is independent of XX, that is, I⁡(MT,X)=0I(M_{T};X)=0.

This protects the rows indexed by TT jointly, including relationships among them. We relax independence using total variation, which measures the largest difference between the probabilities that two distributions assign to the same event. We require the joint distribution of MTM_{T} and XX to be close to the distribution they would have if they were independent.

Definition 4 ([23]).

For T⊆[n]T\subseteq[n] and ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0, the messages M1,…,MnM_{1},\ldots,M_{n} satisfy ε\varepsilon-approximate TT-individual security with respect to XX if dTV​(PMT,X,PMT​PX)≤εd_{\mathrm{TV}}(P_{M_{T},X},P_{M_{T}}P_{X})\leq\varepsilon, where dTV​(P,Q)=12​∑z|P⁡(z)−Q⁡(z)|d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{z}|P(z)-Q(z)| is the total variation distance. The case ε=0\varepsilon=0 recovers TT-individual security.

For a fixed set T⊆[n]T\subseteq[n], let ATA_{T} be the matrix formed by the rows indexed by TT. The following theorem bounds what the entire upload reveals about these rows jointly.

Theorem 3.

Fix T⊆[n]T\subseteq[n] with |T|≤r|T|\leq r. For Low-Rank Factors, dTV​(PAT,X,PAT​PX)≤q|T|−rq−1d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P_{A_{T},X},P_{A_{T}}P_{X})\leq\frac{q^{|T|-r}}{q-1}. For Low-Rank Ball, dTV​(PAT,X,PAT​PX)≤q|T|−rq−1+βn,rd_{\mathrm{TV}}(P_{A_{T},X},P_{A_{T}}P_{X})\leq\frac{q^{|T|-r}}{q-1}+\beta_{n,r}, where βn,r\beta_{n,r} is the probability that a Low-Rank Ball mask has rank less than rr. The same bounds hold when TT indexes columns.

Thus, both sampling methods provide approximate TT-individual security for any fixed set TT of at most rr rows or columns. For fixed qq, the error bound for Low-Rank Factors decreases exponentially with r−|T|r-|T|.

2.5 Maximal-Correlation Secrecy

We now ask how much the server can improve its estimates of functions of the inputs. Maximal-correlation secrecy [18] bounds this improvement for all functions, including those that depend on both matrices. Let MM denote the data we wish to protect, such as AA or the pair (A,B)(A,B), and let 𝒯\mathcal{T} denote the server’s observation. We compare a function f⁡(M)f(M) of the data with a function g⁡(𝒯)g(\mathcal{T}) computed from the observation.

Definition 5 ([18]).

For real-valued random variables F,GF,G with positive variance, their correlation is

Corr⁡(F,G)=𝔼⁡[F​G]−𝔼⁡[F]​𝔼​[G]Var⁡(F)​Var⁡(G).\operatorname{Corr}(F,G)=\frac{\mathbb{E}[FG]-\mathbb{E}[F]\mathbb{E}[G]}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(F)\operatorname{Var}(G)}}.

The maximal correlation ρm​(M,𝒯)\rho_{\mathrm{m}}(M;\mathcal{T}) is the supremum of |Corr⁡(f⁡(M),g⁡(𝒯))||\operatorname{Corr}(f(M),g(\mathcal{T}))| over real-valued functions f,gf,g for which f⁡(M)f(M) and g⁡(𝒯)g(\mathcal{T}) have positive variance. The protocol provides ρ\rho-maximal-correlation secrecy if ρm​(M,𝒯)≤ρ\rho_{\mathrm{m}}(M;\mathcal{T})\leq\rho when MM is uniform.

Maximal correlation is zero exactly when the data and the observation are independent. More generally, a bound ρm​(M,𝒯)≤ρ\rho_{\mathrm{m}}(M;\mathcal{T})\leq\rho means that the observation can reduce the mean-square error in estimating any function of MM by at most a ρ2\rho^{2} fraction of the error of the best estimate based only on the prior. We next bound maximal correlation for both sampling methods against the complete server view 𝒯=(X,Y,Z)\mathcal{T}=(X,Y,Z). Since Z=X​YZ=XY is determined by the uploads, it provides no additional information beyond X,YX,Y.

Theorem 4.

Let AA be uniform over 𝔽qn×n\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n\times n} and let 1≤r<n1\leq r<n. For either sampling method, with RR independent of AA, we have ρm​(A,A+R)≤q−r\rho_{\mathrm{m}}(A;A+R)\leq q^{-r}, with equality for Low-Rank Factors. For independent uniform A,B∈𝔽qn×nA,B\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n\times n} and independent masks R,SR,S sampled using the same method and rank parameter rr, independently of (A,B)(A,B), we have ρm​((A,B),𝒯)=ρm​(A,X)\rho_{\mathrm{m}}((A,B);\mathcal{T})=\rho_{\mathrm{m}}(A;X).

The bound limits how much the server can improve its guesses about the inputs. For example, over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}, a given entry of a uniform matrix AA is equally likely to be zero or one. Before seeing the uploads, the server can guess its value correctly with probability 1/21/2. After seeing the complete view 𝒯\mathcal{T}, this probability is at most 1/2+2−r−11/2+2^{-r-1}. For r=10<nr=10<n, it is less than 50.05%50.05\%, even if the server has unlimited computational power. More generally, for any fixed binary function of (A,B)(A,B), the improvement over the best guess based on the prior is at most q−r/2q^{-r}/2 [18].

The user can make the server’s improvement over the best prior guess tend to zero as the matrices grow, while keeping encoding and decoding close to quadratic. Fix c>0c>0, and set r=⌈c​logq​n⌉r=\lceil c\log_{q}n\rceil. Then, the maximal correlation is at most n−cn^{-c} with O⁡(n2​log⁡n)O(n^{2}\log n) field operations for sufficiently large nn.

We next show that the bound q−rq^{-r} is asymptotically optimal for fixed qq and r=o⁡(n)r=o(n). The converse holds for every input-independent additive mask of rank at most rr, even when combined with secret invertible transformations.

Theorem 5.

Let AA be uniform over 𝔽qn×n\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n\times n} and let X=L1​(A+K)​L2X=L_{1}(A+K)L_{2}, where (L1,L2,K)(L_{1},L_{2},K) is independent of AA, L1,L2L_{1},L_{2} are invertible, and rank⁡(K)≤r≤n−2\operatorname{rank}(K)\leq r\leq n-2 almost surely. Then

ρm​(A,X)≥q2​n−r−2​qn+1(qn−1)2≥q−r2.\rho_{\mathrm{m}}(A;X)\geq\frac{q^{2n-r}-2q^{n}+1}{(q^{n}-1)^{2}}\geq\frac{q^{-r}}{2}. (3)

The server can ignore additional observations, so any view 𝒯\mathcal{T} containing XX satisfies ρm​((A,B),𝒯)≥ρm​(A,X)\rho_{\mathrm{m}}((A,B);\mathcal{T})\geq\rho_{\mathrm{m}}(A;X). The lower bound therefore also applies to the complete server view. Together with Theorem 4, this shows that both sampling methods are within a factor of two of the optimum for r≤n−2r\leq n-2. For fixed qq and r=o⁡(n)r=o(n), the lower bound is (1−o⁡(1))​q−r(1-o(1))q^{-r}, proving asymptotic optimality within this class.

Although Theorem 4 assumes independent uniform inputs, its guessing guarantee extends to nonuniform or correlated inputs. The bound then depends on how concentrated the joint input distribution is. For M=(A,B)M=(A,B), define Δ=log2(q2​n2∑mPr[M=m]2)\Delta=\log_{2}\bigl(q^{2n^{2}}\sum_{m}\Pr[M=m]^{2}\bigr), which is zero for independent uniform inputs. For either sampling method, the improvement over the best prior guess is at most 2Δ/2​q−r2^{\Delta/2}q^{-r} for any fixed function of MM, and half this for a binary function [18, Thm. 1].

3 Proofs

Proof of Theorems 1 and 2.

Since Z=A​B+A​S+R​B+R​SZ=AB+AS+RB+RS, decoding returns A​BAB. Computing R​S=U⁡((V​Q)​W)RS=U((VQ)W) and using r≤min⁡{m,n,p}r\leq\min\{m,n,p\} gives the cost bound. Uniform rank-ball masks give a constant likelihood on compatible inputs and zero elsewhere, so Bayes’ rule gives both posterior statements. ∎

Let Cd,e​(t)=∏j=0t−1(qd−qj)​(qe−qj)qt−qjC_{d,e}(t)=\prod_{j=0}^{t-1}\frac{(q^{d}-q^{j})(q^{e}-q^{j})}{q^{t}-q^{j}} count rank-tt matrices and put Vd,e​(r)=∑t=0rCd,e​(t)V_{d,e}(r)=\sum_{t=0}^{r}C_{d,e}(t). To sample a Low-Rank Ball mask, choose tt with probability Cd,e​(t)/Vd,e​(r)C_{d,e}(t)/V_{d,e}(r), then multiply independent uniform full-rank factors of sizes d×td\times t and t×et\times e. Each rank-tt matrix has equally many such factorizations, so the product is uniform. Pad the factors to width rr, i.e., inserting zeros. Rejection sampling takes O⁡((d+e)​r2)O((d+e)r^{2}) expected field operations offline, excluding integer arithmetic for the rank probabilities. Write Cn=Cn,nC_{n}=C_{n,n} and Vn=Vn,nV_{n}=V_{n,n}.

Proof of Proposition 1.

For each entry ii, let hi​(K−i)h_{i}(K_{-i}) be a most likely value of KiK_{i} given the others and put pi=Pr[Ki=hi(K−i)]p_{i}=\Pr[K_{i}=h_{i}(K_{-i})]. Apply DP to the event xi=hi​(x−i)x_{i}=h_{i}(x_{-i}), comparing zero with every nonzero change to entry ii. Summing gives (q−1)​pi≤eε​(1−pi)+(q−1)​δ(q-1)p_{i}\leq e^{\varepsilon}(1-p_{i})+(q-1)\delta. A distribution whose largest probability is pp has entropy at least 2​(1−p)2(1-p) bits. Applying this conditionally and using the chain rule gives H⁡(K)≥∑iH⁡(Ki∣K−i)≥2​n2​(q−1)​(1−δ)eε+q−1H(K)\geq\sum_{i}H(K_{i}\mid K_{-i})\geq\frac{2n^{2}(q-1)(1-\delta)}{e^{\varepsilon}+q-1}. Counting factor pairs gives H⁡(K)≤2​n​r​log2​qH(K)\leq 2nr\log_{2}q, proving (2). For δ=0\delta=0, singleton events make the support invariant under every entry translation, forcing full support and contradicting r<nr<n. ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.

Put k=|T|k=|T|. Since AA is uniform, XX and RR are independent. Given X=xX=x, we have AT=xT−RTA_{T}=x_{T}-R_{T}, so the required distance equals the distance of RTR_{T} from uniform. Write pk,d=∏j=0k−1(1−qj−d)p_{k,d}=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(1-q^{j-d}). For Low-Rank Factors, UT​VU_{T}V is uniform when UTU_{T} has full row rank, an event of probability pk,rp_{k,r}. The distance is therefore at most 1−pk,r≤qk−r/(q−1)1-p_{k,r}\leq q^{k-r}/(q-1).

For uniform rank-rr masks, use full-rank factors. Then rank⁡(RT)=rank⁡(UT)\operatorname{rank}(R_{T})=\operatorname{rank}(U_{T}). Conditioning a uniform n×rn\times r matrix UU on having full column rank gives Pr[rank(RT)=k]=Pr[rank(UT)=k∣rank(U)=r]=pk,r​pr−k,n−kpr,n=pk,rpk,n\Pr[\operatorname{rank}(R_{T})=k]=\Pr[\operatorname{rank}(U_{T})=k\mid\operatorname{rank}(U)=r]=\frac{p_{k,r}p_{r-k,n-k}}{p_{r,n}}=\frac{p_{k,r}}{p_{k,n}}, where the last equality uses pr,n=pk,n​pr−k,n−kp_{r,n}=p_{k,n}p_{r-k,n-k}. Conditional on full row rank, RTR_{T} is uniform by invariance under invertible column operations. A uniform k×nk\times n matrix has the same conditional law, with event probability pk,np_{k,n}. Both probabilities are at least pk,rp_{k,r}, giving a distance of at most 1−pk,r1-p_{k,r}. Mixing lower ranks adds at most βn,r=Vn​(r−1)/Vn​(r)\beta_{n,r}=V_{n}(r-1)/V_{n}(r). Transposition gives the column bounds. ∎

Proof of Theorem 4.

Let χH​(M)=ψ⁡(∑i​jHi​j​Mi​j)\chi_{H}(M)=\psi(\sum_{ij}H_{ij}M_{ij}), where ψ\psi is a nontrivial additive character of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. These characters form an orthonormal basis, and 𝔼⁡[χH​(A)∣X=x]=χH​(x)​𝔼​[χH​(R)]¯\mathbb{E}[\chi_{H}(A)\mid X=x]=\chi_{H}(x)\overline{\mathbb{E}[\chi_{H}(R)]}. Thus, conditional expectation is diagonal, giving ρm​(A,X)=maxH≠0⁡|𝔼⁡[χH​(R)]|\rho_{\mathrm{m}}(A;X)=\max_{H\neq 0}|\mathbb{E}[\chi_{H}(R)]|. For Low-Rank Factors, averaging over VV gives 𝔼[χH(UV)]=Pr[HTU=0]=q−r​rank⁡(H)\mathbb{E}[\chi_{H}(UV)]=\Pr[H^{T}U=0]=q^{-r\operatorname{rank}(H)}, with maximum q−rq^{-r}.

For Low-Rank Ball, invariance under invertible row and column operations lets us take H=diag⁡(1,H′)H=\operatorname{diag}(1,H^{\prime}) for H≠0H\neq 0. Write M=(abcD)M=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\ c&D\end{smallmatrix}\right). For fixed b,c,Db,c,D with rank⁡(D)<r\operatorname{rank}(D)<r, either every aa satisfies the rank bound or none does, so the sum over aa vanishes. When rank⁡(D)=r\operatorname{rank}(D)=r, the rank bound requires b,cb,c in its row and column spaces and, after reducing DD to diag⁡(Ir,0)\operatorname{diag}(I_{r},0), fixes a=b1​c1a=b_{1}c_{1}. Proof of Theorem 5.

Let g⁡(A)=|ker⁡A|=qn−rank⁡(A)g(A)=|\ker A|=q^{n-\operatorname{rank}(A)} and N=qnN=q^{n}. Both A,XA,X are uniform, and rank invariance gives g⁡(X)=g⁡(A+K)g(X)=g(A+K).
